example: Jah, ma tulen. — Yes, I'm coming.
Ei, aitäh. — No, thank you.
Mina ja sina. — You and I.
Kas kohv või tee? — Coffee or tea?
Ilm on ilus, aga külm. — The weather is nice but cold.
Ma jään koju, sest sajab vihma. — I'm staying home because it's raining.
Ma tean, et sa oled väsinud. — I know you're tired. • Ma tulin, et sind aidata. — I came to help you.
Kui sul on aega, helista. — If you have time, call me. • Ta on pikem kui mina. — He is taller than I am.
notes: Three meanings: if, when and than (in comparisons). Also used in kui palju? (how much/many?) and kui vana? (how old?).

example: Mis see on? — What is this? • Mis värvi see on? — What colour is it?
notes: Can mean both what? and which? Forms include mida (object), mille (genitive), millega (with what) and millest (about what).

example: Kes see on? — Who is this? • Kes seal on? — Who's there?
notes: Forms include keda (object: who), kelle (whose), kellele (to whom), kellel (who has) and kellega (with whom).

example: Kus sa elad? — Where do you live? • Kus on tualett? — Where is the toilet?
notes: Answers often use the -s or -l location ending: koolis (at school), tööl (at work).

example: Kuhu sa lähed? — Where are you going? • Kuhu me läheme? — Where shall we go?
notes: Answers often use a destination ending such as -sse or -le: poodi (to the shop), tööle (to work), koju (home).

example: Kust sa tuled? — Where are you coming from? • Kust sa pärit oled? — Where are you from?
notes: Answers often use -st or -lt: poest (from the shop), töölt (from work).

example: Millal sa tuled? — When are you coming? • Millal pood kinni läheb? — When does the shop close?
notes: For an exact time, mis kell? (at what time?) is more common.

example: Miks sa naerad? — Why are you laughing? • Miks sa ei tulnud? — Why didn't you come?
notes: A typical answer starts with sest (because).

example: Kuidas läheb? — How are things? • Kuidas see eesti keeles on? — How do you say this in Estonian?
Mitu last sul on? — How many children do you have? • Mitu piletit sa ostsid? — How many tickets did you buy?
notes: Used to ask how many. The following noun is in the singular partitive: mitu last (how many children), mitu korda (how many times).

example: Milline kleit on ilusam? — Which dress is prettier? • Milline on sinu lemmikvärv? — What's your favourite colour?
notes: Also missugune. In everyday speech, mis is often used instead.

example: See on minu maja. — This is my house. • See raamat on huvitav. — This book is interesting.
notes: Forms: seda (object), selle (genitive), sellega (with this). Plural: need (these).

example: See või too? — This one or that one?
Ma olen siin. — I'm here.
Pood on seal. — The shop is over there.
Mina olen Anna. — I'm Anna. • Mina ka! — Me too!
notes: Short form: ma. Related forms: minu/mu (my), mind (me), mulle (to me), mul (I have, with on), minuga (with me).

example: Kas sina oled Mark? — Are you Mark? • Sina oled mu parim sõber. — You're my best friend.
notes: Short form: sa. Related forms: sinu/su (your), sind (you, object), sulle (to you), sul (you have, with on), sinuga (with you).

example: Tema on minu õde. — She's my sister. • Tema auto on punane. — His car is red.
notes: Short form: ta. Estonian does not distinguish he and she. Forms: tema (genitive), teda (object), talle (to him/her), tal (he/she has, with on), temaga (with him/her).

example: Meie oleme sõbrad. — We're friends. • Meie kodu on siin lähedal. — Our home is nearby.
notes: Short form: me. Also means our. Forms: meid (us), meile (to us), meil (we have, with on), meiega (with us).

example: Kas teie olete arst? — Are you a doctor? • Kas see on teie kott? — Is this your bag?
notes: Short form: te. Used both for plural you and polite singular you; can also mean your. Forms: teid, teile, teil and teiega.

example: Nemad elavad Tartus. — They live in Tartu. • Nemad on minu sõbrad. — They're my friends.
notes: Short form: nad. Forms: nende (their), neid (them), neile (to them), neil (they have, with on), nendega (with them).

example: See on minu raamat. — This is my book. • Minu ema on arst. — My mother is a doctor.
Kus on sinu kott? — Where's your bag? • Sinu eesti keel on väga hea. — Your Estonian is very good.
Kõik on korras. — Everything is fine. • Kõik on siin. — Everyone is here.
notes: Refers to all people (everyone) or all things (everything).

example: Kas sa tahad midagi juua? — Would you like something to drink? • Ma ei taha midagi. — I don't want anything.
notes: In a negative sentence, it means anything/nothing: ma ei näe midagi — I can't see anything.

example: Keegi koputab. — Someone is knocking. • Kas keegi on kodus? — Is anyone home?
notes: In a negative sentence, keegi ei tea means nobody knows.

example: Ma jooksen iga päev. — I go running every day.
Mul on palju tööd. — I have a lot of work to do. • Palju õnne! — Congratulations! (Happy birthday!)
notes: Followed by the partitive: palju tööd (a lot of work), palju inimesi (many people).

example: Mul on vähe aega. — I don't have much time.
Ma räägin natuke eesti keelt. — I speak a little Estonian.
Väga hea! — Very good!
Mina tulen ka. — I'm coming too. • Ka mina tulen. — I'm coming as well.
Kas sa tahad veel kohvi? — Would you like some more coffee? • Ma ei ole veel söönud. — I haven't eaten yet.
notes: In negatives, often means yet: ma ei ole veel söönud — I haven't eaten yet.

example: Ma olen juba kodus. — I'm already home. • Kas sa juba sõid? — Have you eaten already?
Mul on ainult üks vend. — I only have one brother.
Võib-olla homme. — Maybe tomorrow.
Muidugi aitan! — Of course I'll help!
See on tähtis asi. — This is an important matter.
Kas see koht on vaba? — Is this seat available?
Elu on ilus. — Life is beautiful.
Tere, kuidas läheb? — Hi, how are you? • Tere hommikust! — Good morning!
Tervist, härra Kask! — Hello, Mr Kask!
notes: A greeting for any time of day, literally '(I wish you) health'. After a sneeze, Estonians usually say Terviseks!

example: Aitäh abi eest! — Thank you for your help! • Aitäh, väga maitsev! — Thank you, it was delicious!
Tänan väga! — Thank you very much!
notes: A little more formal than aitäh.

english: please; here you are; you're welcome
example: Üks kohv, palun. — One coffee, please. • Palun, võtke istet. — Please have a seat.
notes: Also a reply to aitäh (thank you): palun — you're welcome.

example: Vabandust, kus on jaam? — Excuse me, where is the station? • Vabandust, ma hilinesin. — Sorry I'm late.
Nägemist, homseni! — Goodbye, see you tomorrow!
Kohtumiseni reedel! — See you on Friday!
Terviseks! — Cheers!
Appi! Aidake! — Help! Somebody help!
Telefoninumber algab nulliga. — The phone number starts with zero.
Mul on üks õde. — I have one sister.
Mul on kaks kassi. — I have two cats.
Meil on kolm last. — We have three children.
Kell on neli. — It's four o'clock.
Viis eurot, palun. — Five euros, please.
Ma ärkan kell kuus. — I wake up at six.
notes: Do not confuse with kuu (month, moon).

example: Kolm pluss neli on seitse. — Three plus four is seven.
Tööpäev on kaheksa tundi. — The working day is eight hours long.
Pood avatakse kell üheksa. — The shop opens at nine.
Mul on kümme eurot. — I have ten euros.
Kell on üksteist. — It's eleven o'clock.
Aastas on kaksteist kuud. — There are twelve months in a year.
Ta on kakskümmend aastat vana. — He's twenty years old.
See maksab sada eurot. — It costs one hundred euros.
See maksab tuhat eurot. — It costs a thousand euros.
See on minu esimene päev. — This is my first day.
Ma elan teisel korrusel. — I live on the second floor. • Anna mulle teine tass, palun. — Please give me another cup.
notes: Can mean second or another, depending on context.

example: Täna on kolmas mai. — Today is the third of May.
Kell on pool kaks. — It's half past one. • Pool leiba, palun. — Half a loaf of bread, please.
notes: When telling time, pool kaks means 1:30 (half past one), not 2:30.

example: Mis on sinu telefoninumber? — What's your phone number?
Mul pole aega. — I don't have time. • Mis ajal sa tuled? — What time are you coming?
notes: Forms: aja (genitive), aega (partitive). Mis ajal? — At what time? Mul pole aega. — I have no time.

example: Head päeva! — Have a nice day!
Head ööd! — Good night!
Hommik on külm. — It's a cold morning.
Lõunal sööme koos. — We'll eat lunch together. • Lähme lõunale! — Let's go for lunch! • Tartu on Tallinnast lõunas. — Tartu is south of Tallinn.
Tere õhtust! — Good evening! • Head õhtut! — Have a nice evening!
Ma olen nädal aega puhkusel. — I'm on holiday for a week.
Ma maksan üüri kord kuus. — I pay rent once a month. • Täna on täiskuu. — There's a full moon tonight.
Head uut aastat! — Happy New Year!
Ma ootan juba tund aega. — I've been waiting for an hour already. • Eesti keele tund algab kell kümme. — The Estonian lesson starts at ten.
Oota üks minut. — Wait a minute.
Kell on viis. — It's five o'clock. • Mul on uus kell. — I have a new watch.
notes: Can refer to a clock or watch. Kell kolm means at three o'clock.

example: Täna on reede. — Today is Friday. • Täna õhtul lähen kinno. — I'm going to the cinema this evening.
Homme on puhkepäev. — Tomorrow is a day off.
Eile sadas vihma. — It rained yesterday.
Nüüd ma saan aru. — Now I understand.
Ma olen praegu tööl. — I'm at work right now.
Ma tulen kohe. — I'll be right there.
Varsti on suvi. — Summer will be here soon.
Helistan sulle hiljem. — I'll call you later.
Ta on alati rõõmus. — She's always cheerful.
Ma käin tihti ujumas. — I often go swimming.
Mõnikord ma töötan kodus. — Sometimes I work from home.
notes: Made up of mõni (some) + kord (time, occasion).

english: ever, at some time; never (with a negative)
example: Ma pole kunagi Pariisis käinud. — I've never been to Paris.
notes: With a negative, ei kunagi means never.

example: Hommikul joon kohvi. — I drink coffee in the morning.
Õhtul vaatan filmi. — I watch a film in the evening.
Pese käed enne sööki. — Wash your hands before eating.
Pärast tööd lähen poodi. — I go to the shop after work.
Esmaspäeval algab töönädal. — The working week starts on Monday.
Teisipäeval on mul eesti keele tund. — I have an Estonian lesson on Tuesday.
Kolmapäeval käin ujumas. — I go swimming on Wednesdays.
Neljapäeval tuleb ema külla. — Mum is coming to visit on Thursday.
Reedel läheme kinno. — We're going to the cinema on Friday.
Laupäeval ma puhkan. — I rest on Saturdays.
Pühapäeval on pood kinni. — The shop is closed on Sundays.

Kevad on tulnud. — Spring has arrived.
Suvi on soe. — Summer is warm.
Sügisel on palju vihma. — It rains a lot in autumn.
Talv on pikk ja külm. — Winter is long and cold.
Ta on hea inimene. — He's a good person.
See mees on minu isa. — That man is my father.

Laps magab. — The child is sleeping.
Poiss mängib jalgpalli. — The boy is playing football.
Tüdruk loeb raamatut. — The girl is reading a book.
Meil on suur pere. — We have a big family.
Minu ema on arst. — My mother is a doctor.
Isa on tööl. — Dad is at work.
Mu vanemad elavad maal. — My parents live in the countryside.
notes: Plural form of vanem (parent; also older).

example: Meie poeg käib koolis. — Our son goes to school.
Tütar on viieaastane. — Our daughter is five years old.
Mu vend elab Soomes. — My brother lives in Finland.
Mul on kaks õde. — I have two sisters.
notes: Can also mean a nurse (especially in compound forms).

example: Vanaema küpsetab kooki. — Grandma is baking a cake.
Vanaisa loeb ajalehte. — Grandpa is reading the newspaper.
Ta on minu parim sõber. — He's my best friend.
Mis su nimi on? — What's your name?
Toit on valmis. — The food is ready.
Klaas vett, palun. — A glass of water, please.
Ma joon piima. — I drink milk.
Kas sa tahad kohvi? — Would you like some coffee?
Ma joon teed sidruniga. — I drink tea with lemon.
notes: Also means road or way (a separate word with the same spelling).

Üks õlu, palun. — One beer, please.
Kas punane või valge vein? — Red or white wine?
Eesti must leib on maitsev. — Estonian dark rye bread is delicious.
notes: White bread is called sai; leib usually means darker rye bread.

example: Ma ostan saia. — I'm buying some white bread.
Leib võiga. — Bread with butter.
notes: The same spelling also means or (a separate word).

example: Võileib juustuga. — A cheese sandwich.
Ma söön hommikul muna. — I eat an egg for breakfast.
Ma ei söö liha. — I don't eat meat.
Täna on õhtuks kana. — We're having chicken for dinner tonight.
Mulle meeldib kala. — I like fish.
Võileival on vorst. — There's sausage on the sandwich.
Kartul on keedetud. — The potatoes are boiled.
Õun on punane. — The apple is red.
Ahv sööb banaani. — The monkey is eating a banana.
Salatis on tomat. — There's tomato in the salad.
Ma lõikan kurki. — I'm slicing a cucumber.
Supp on kuum. — The soup is hot.
Ma teen salatit. — I'm making a salad.
Kohv ilma suhkruta. — Coffee without sugar.
Anna mulle soola. — Pass me the salt, please.
See kook on väga hea. — This cake is delicious.
Lapsed söövad jäätist. — The children are eating ice cream.
Mulle meeldib šokolaad. — I love chocolate.
Söö iga päev puuvilju. — Eat fruit every day.
Köögiviljad on tervislikud. — Vegetables are good for you.
Hommikusöök on valmis. — Breakfast is ready.
Lõunasöök on kell kaksteist. — Lunch is at twelve.
Mis on õhtusöögiks? — What's for dinner?
Minu kodu on Tallinnas. — My home is in Tallinn.
Ma olen kodus. — I'm at home.
Ma lähen koju. — I'm going home.
See maja on vana. — This house is old.
Meil on kolmetoaline korter. — We have a three-room flat.
Minu tuba on väike. — My room is small.
Ema on köögis. — Mum is in the kitchen.
Vannituba on vaba. — The bathroom is free.
Kus on tualett? — Where's the toilet?
Sulge uks, palun. — Please close the door.
Ava aken. — Open the window.
Raamat on laual. — The book is on the table.
Istu toolile. — Sit on the chair.
Laps on voodis. — The child is in bed.
Riided on kapis. — The clothes are in the wardrobe.
Kass magab diivanil. — The cat is sleeping on the sofa.
Aias kasvavad lilled. — Flowers grow in the garden.
Kus on minu võti? — Where's my key?
Tallinn on ilus linn. — Tallinn is a beautiful city.
Ma elan Pikal tänaval. — I live on Pikk Street.
Pood on lahti. — The shop is open.
Ostame turult maasikaid. — Let's buy strawberries at the market.
Kohtume kohvikus. — Let's meet at the café.
Me sööme restoranis. — We're eating at a restaurant.
Hotell on mere ääres. — The hotel is by the sea.
Pank on avatud kella viieni. — The bank is open until five.
Apteek on nurga taga. — The pharmacy is around the corner.
Ta on haiglas. — He's in hospital.
Lapsed lähevad kooli. — The children are going to school.
Ta õpib ülikoolis. — She's studying at university.
Me jalutame pargis. — We're walking in the park.
Läheme kinno! — Let's go to the cinema!
Täna õhtul läheme teatrisse. — We're going to the theatre tonight.
Rong on jaamas. — The train is at the station.
Kuidas saada lennujaama? — How do I get to the airport?
Mul on uus auto. — I have a new car.
Buss tuleb kümne minuti pärast. — The bus will arrive in ten minutes.
Rong läheb Tartusse. — The train is going to Tartu.
Ma sõidan trammiga. — I'm taking the tram.
Kutsu takso, palun. — Please call a taxi.
Lennuk lendab Londonisse. — The plane is flying to London.
Laev sõidab Helsingisse. — The ferry is going to Helsinki.
Ma sõidan jalgrattaga tööle. — I cycle to work.
Tee on pikk. — It's a long road. • Kas see on õige tee? — Is this the right way?
notes: The same spelling also means tea (a separate word).

example: Üks pilet Tartusse, palun. — One ticket to Tartu, please.
Järgmine peatus on kesklinn. — The next stop is the city centre.
Pööra vasakule. — Turn left.
Mine paremale. — Go right.
Mine otse edasi. — Go straight ahead.
Kas jaam on kaugel? — Is the station far away?
Pood on lähedal. — The shop is nearby.
Mis värvi on sinu auto? — What colour is your car?
Lumi on valge. — Snow is white.
Mul on must kass. — I have a black cat.
Roos on punane. — The rose is red.
Taevas on sinine. — The sky is blue.
Muru on roheline. — The grass is green.
Päike on kollane. — The sun is yellow.
Täna on hall ilm. — It's grey and overcast today.
Tal on pruunid silmad. — He has brown eyes.
Tüdrukul on roosa kleit. — The girl has a pink dress.
See on hea raamat. — This is a good book. • Hea küll! — All right!
Täna on halb ilm. — The weather is bad today.
Sa räägid hästi eesti keelt. — You speak Estonian well.
Ma magasin halvasti. — I slept badly.
Meil on suur maja. — We have a big house.
Mul on väike koer. — I have a small dog.
Mul on uus telefon. — I have a new phone.
See auto on vana. — This car is old.
Ta on veel noor. — He's still young.
Sa oled ilus. — You're beautiful.
See on pikk lugu. — It's a long story. • Ta on väga pikk. — He's very tall.
Päev on talvel lühike. — The days are short in winter.
See maja on väga kõrge. — This building is very tall.
See kleit on liiga kallis. — This dress is too expensive.
Siin on odav. — It's cheap here.
Mul on kiire. — I'm in a hurry.
notes: Mul on kiire means I'm in a hurry.

example: Internet on aeglane. — The internet is slow.
Eesti keel on raske. — Estonian is difficult.
Kott on kerge. — The bag is light.
See on lihtne. — It's simple.
See on õige vastus. — That's the right answer.
See on vale number. — That's the wrong number.
Tee on kuum. — The tea is hot.
See on tore! — That's great!
See film on huvitav. — This film is interesting.
Ma olen väga väsinud. — I'm very tired.
Ma olen haige. — I'm ill.
Laps on jälle terve. — The child is healthy again.
Söök on valmis. — The food is ready.
Kas see koht on vaba? — Is this seat free?
Ma olen eestlane. — I'm Estonian. • Siin on pood. — There's a shop here.
notes: ma olen — I am; sa oled — you are; ta on — he/she is; ma olin — I was; ei ole/pole — am/is/are not.

example: Ma lähen tööle. — I'm going to work. • Kuidas läheb? — How are things going?
notes: ma lähen — I go/am going; ma läksin — I went; mine! — Go!

example: Tule siia! — Come here!
Mida sa teed? — What are you doing? • Ma teen süüa. — I'm cooking.
notes: ma teen — I do/make; ma tegin — I did/made; tee! — Do it!

english: to get, to be able to, to become
example: Kas ma saan aidata? — Can I help? • Ma sain kingituse. — I got a present. • Temast saab arst. — He's going to become a doctor.
notes: ma saan — I get/can. Saan aru means I understand; temast saab means he/she will become.

example: Ma tahan süüa. — I want to eat. • Ma tahan koju. — I want to go home.
notes: ma tahan — I want. Followed by a -da infinitive: tahan süüa — I want to eat.

english: to be allowed to; can, may
example: Kas ma võin sisse tulla? — May I come in? • Kas ma võin akna avada? — May I open the window?
notes: ma võin — I may/can; võib — it is allowed. Compare oskama (have a skill) and saama (be able to).

example: Ma pean minema. — I have to go. • Sa pead puhkama. — You need to rest.
notes: ma pean — I must/have to. Followed by a -ma infinitive: pean minema — I have to go.

english: to know how to, to be able to
example: Kas sa oskad ujuda? — Can you swim? • Ma oskan natuke eesti keelt. — I speak a little Estonian.
notes: ma oskan — I know how to. Oskan eesti keelt means I speak/know Estonian.

example: Ma ei tea. — I don't know. • Kas sa tead, kus ta elab? — Do you know where he lives?
notes: ma tean — I know. Teadma is for facts; tundma is for knowing a person or being familiar with something.

example: Ma armastan sind. — I love you.
Mulle meeldib muusika. — I like music. • Kas sulle meeldib siin? — Do you like it here?
notes: mulle meeldib — I like (literally: it pleases me). The person liking something takes an -le form.

example: Ma elan Tallinnas. — I live in Tallinn.
Ta töötab haiglas. — She works at a hospital.
Ma õpin eesti keelt. — I'm learning Estonian. • Ma õpin ülikoolis. — I'm studying at university.
Ma loen raamatut. — I'm reading a book.
Ma kirjutan kirja. — I'm writing a letter.
Kas sa räägid inglise keelt? — Do you speak English? • Räägi aeglasemalt, palun. — Please speak more slowly.
Mida sa ütlesid? — What did you say? • Ütle, palun, kus on jaam. — Please tell me where the station is.
Võin ma küsida? — May I ask a question?
Palun vasta küsimusele. — Please answer the question.
Ma kuulan muusikat. — I'm listening to music.
Ma näen sind. — I can see you. • Head nägemist! — Goodbye!
Me vaatame filmi. — We're watching a film.
Mida sa sööd? — What are you eating?
Ma joon vett. — I'm drinking water.
Laps magab. — The child is sleeping.
Istu, palun. — Please sit down.
Ta seisab akna juures. — He's standing by the window.

english: to go regularly, to attend, to visit
example: Ma käin iga päev tööl. — I go to work every day. • Ma käin poes. — I go to the shop.
notes: ma käin — I go regularly/visit. Käin poes can mean I'm popping to the shop (and coming back).

example: Ta jookseb pargis. — She's running in the park.

english: to travel by vehicle, to drive, to ride
example: Me sõidame bussiga. — We're travelling by bus. • Ma sõidan homme Tartusse. — I'm going to Tartu tomorrow.
notes: ma sõidan — I travel by vehicle/drive/ride.

example: Ma ostan leiba. — I'm buying bread.
Kui palju see maksab? — How much does it cost? • Kas ma saan kaardiga maksta? — Can I pay by card?
notes: ma maksan — I pay; see maksab — it costs.

example: Anna mulle pliiats. — Give me a pencil. • Anna andeks! — Sorry!
notes: ma annan — I give; anna! — Give!; anna andeks — Forgive me!/Sorry!

example: Võta üks komm. — Have a sweet. • Võta aega! — Take your time!
Pane raamat lauale. — Put the book on the table. • Pane jope selga. — Put your jacket on.
Ava uks! — Open the door!
Ma helistan sulle õhtul. — I'll call you this evening. • Helista mulle! — Call me!
notes: ma helistan — I call. The person you call takes an -le form: helistan emale — I call Mum.

example: Ma ootan sind. — I'm waiting for you. • Oota natuke! — Wait a moment!
Kas sa saad mind aidata? — Can you help me? • Aitäh, et aitasid! — Thank you for helping!
notes: ma aitan — I help. The person helped takes the partitive: aita mind — Help me.

example: Lapsed mängivad õues. — The children are playing outside.
Ta laulab hästi. — She sings well.
Ma ujun meres. — I'm swimming in the sea.
Ma pesen käsi. — I'm washing my hands.

example: Üks kümnendik meetrist on kümme sentimeetrit. — One tenth of a metre is ten centimetres.
notes: After üks, use the nominative: kümnendik. With cardinal numbers greater than one, use the partitive: kümnendikku.

example: Kolm kümnendikku on 0,3. — Three tenths equals 0.3.
notes: kümnendikku is the singular partitive of kümnendik, used after kolm.

example: Seitse kümnendikku on 0,7. — Seven tenths equals 0.7.
notes: kümnendikku is the singular partitive of kümnendik, used after seitse.

example: Üheksa kümnendikku on 0,9. — Nine tenths equals 0.9.
notes: kümnendikku is the singular partitive of kümnendik, used after üheksa.

example: Üks sajandik eurost on üks sent. — One hundredth of a euro is one cent.
notes: After üks, use the nominative: sajandik. With cardinal numbers greater than one, use the partitive: sajandikku.

example: Viis sajandikku on 0,05. — Five hundredths equals 0.05.
notes: sajandikku is the singular partitive of sajandik, used after viis.

example: Kakskümmend viis sajandikku on veerand. — Twenty-five hundredths equals a quarter.
notes: sajandikku is the singular partitive of sajandik, used after kakskümmend viis.

example: Üks tuhandik kilomeetrist on üks meeter. — One thousandth of a kilometre is one metre.
notes: After üks, use the nominative: tuhandik. With cardinal numbers greater than one, use the partitive: tuhandikku.

example: Kaks ja pool tundi on 150 minutit. — Two and a half hours is 150 minutes.
notes: pool means half; kaks ja pool is 2½. With a unit: kaks ja pool tundi.

example: Sõit kestab kolm ja pool tundi. — The journey takes three and a half hours.
notes: pool means half; kolm ja pool is 3½. With a unit: kolm ja pool tundi.

example: Pudelis on üks ja veerand liitrit vett. — The bottle contains one and a quarter litres of water.
notes: veerand means a quarter; üks ja veerand is 1¼. With a unit: üks ja veerand liitrit.

example: Pool on murdarv. — A half is a fraction.
0,25 on kümnendmurd. — 0.25 is a decimal fraction.
notes: Decimal fraction: 0,25 = 25/100. Estonian uses a decimal comma.

example: Üks sent on sajandik eurost. — One cent is a hundredth of a euro.
notes: From sada (hundred). Key forms: sajandik, sajandiku, sajandikku.

example: Üks gramm on tuhandik kilogrammist. — One gram is a thousandth of a kilogram.
notes: From tuhat (thousand). Key forms: tuhandik, tuhandiku, tuhandikku.

example: Kuuendik koogist on alles. — One sixth of the cake is left.
notes: From kuues (sixth). Key forms: kuuendik, kuuendiku, kuuendikku.

example: Kaheksandik liitrist on 125 milliliitrit. — An eighth of a litre is 125 millilitres.
notes: From kaheksas (eighth). Key forms: kaheksandik, kaheksandiku, kaheksandikku.

example: Murru 3/4 nimetaja on neli. — The denominator of 3/4 is four.
notes: Denominator (the bottom number in a fraction); numerator — lugeja.

example: Kümnendmurrus eraldab koma murdosa. — In Estonian, a comma separates the fractional part of a decimal.
notes: Comma in text and the decimal separator in Estonian numbers: 0,9 — null koma üheksa.

example: Laste mänguasjad on põrandal. — The children’s toys are on the floor.
notes: laste is the plural genitive of laps.
